To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the velocity pattern of the IRAS04166+2707 molecular jet is the result of a spherically symmetric wind with an axial density enhancement, and the ejection history can be reconstructed with the unified wind model of Shang et al (2006).

a linearly decreasing velocity profile can naturally arise from the interaction between the jet and wind, and the observed velocity profile of IRAS 041266+2706 can be explained by a unified wind model.
the IRAS 41.7+27.1 jet is a spherically symmetric expanding wind, and the velocity pattern of its knots can be reproduced by the unified wind model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the reconstruction of the ejection history and the formation of the saw tooth pattern of the IRAS04166+2708 jet.
the ejection history, kinematic behavior and physical properties of the jet and outflow driven by the IRAS 41.66+2706 protostar.
the ejection history and geometry of the IRAS04166+2708 jet, and the results can be applied to the other similar jets.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the jet of the IRAS04166+2707 system is a combination of a jet and a wind with the same inclination angle, and the jet is launched in the beginning and then the wind takes over.
the jet is driven by a spheroidally expanding wind with an axial density concentration, and the wind is ejected with a constant velocity of 0.3c.
the IRAS 41.66+2706 system is a young protostar with an age of 1000 years and a mass of $\approx 1 M_{\odot}$.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the IRAS 41 66+2706 jet is likely to be a young and well collimated jet with a low mass loss rate, and its ejection history is consistent with a continuous and slow ejection of a wind with axial density enhancement.
the ejection history can be reconstructed from the position-velocity diagram of the jet through projection.
the IRAS 41.66+27.06 jet is driven by a wind with a constant mass loss rate, and the jet and wind materials are ejected from the same direction with an angle of 52$^\circ$ to the line of sight.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ejection history is not unique.
the observed velocity pattern in the jet is not the ejection history but the projection effect of an expanding wind.
the velocity pattern of the jet is not only determined by the intrinsic ejection history of jet and wind but also the geometry of the system.
